claim: Rem2 expression peaks in the cortex around the time of eye opening (P9-P14, eyes open at P13 in rodents).
source: We found that Rem2 expression peaks in the cortex around the time of eye opening (P9-P14, eyes open at P13 in rodents), and declines near the end of the critical period (P35, (Gordon and Stryker, 1996).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing Rem2 protein levels at different developmental time points (Figure 1A) and quantification showing peak expression at P9-P14.

claim: Rem2 expression declines near the end of the critical period (P35).
source: We found that Rem2 expression peaks in the cortex around the time of eye opening (P9-P14, eyes open at P13 in rodents), and declines near the end of the critical period (P35, (Gordon and Stryker, 1996).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1A showing reduced Rem2 protein levels at P35 compared to earlier time points.

claim: 90 min of light stimulation led to a significant and rapid increase in Rem2 mRNA expression in V1 with no change in Rem2 mRNA expression in S1.
source: Compared to DR littermates, 90 min of light stimulation led to a significant and rapid increase in Rem2 mRNA expression in V1 with no change in Rem2 mRNA expression in S1 (Figure 1B, left).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing fold change in Rem2 mRNA expression in V1 versus S1 following light exposure (Figure 1B).

claim: An increase in mRNA levels of the immediate early gene Fos was observed in response to changes in visual experience.
source: As expected, we also observed an increase in mRNA levels of the immediate early gene Fos in response to changes in visual experience (Figure 1B, right).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing increased Fos mRNA expression following light stimulation (Figure 1B, right).

claim: Rem2 mRNA expression in V1 is modulated by visual stimulation coincident with experience-dependent development of visual cortical circuits.
source: These data illustrate that Rem2 mRNA expression in V1 is modulated by visual stimulation coincident with experience-dependent development of visual cortical circuits.
evidence: Based on the observed increase in Rem2 mRNA following light stimulation in dark-reared mice during the critical period.

claim: Rem2 mRNA expression can be modulated by visual stimulation both at P28 and in the adult visual cortex.
source: Interestingly, although our results demonstrate a reduction in baseline Rem2 protein expression around P28 and in adulthood (Figure 1A, compared to P9 and P14), Rem2 mRNA expression can be modulated by visual stimulation both at P28 (Figure 1B) and in the adult visual cortex (Mardinly et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data at P28 (Figure 1B) and citation to previous work showing adult modulation.

claim: Insertion of the cassette disrupts Rem2 expression at the protein level.
source: We also demonstrated that, as expected (Skarnes et al., 2011), insertion of the cassette disrupts Rem2 expression by immunoblotting (Figure 2C), confirming a null allele at the protein level.
evidence: Supported by Western blot showing absence of Rem2 protein in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 2C).

claim: Rem2-/- mice are viable and fertile and do not display any overt phenotypes.
source: Rem2-/- mice are viable and fertile and do not display any overt phenotypes.
evidence: Based on observation of the knockout mice.

claim: The genotypes of pups obtained from a Rem2+/- cross are recovered in the expected Mendelian ratio.
source: The genotypes of pups obtained from a Rem2+/- cross are recovered in the expected Mendelian ratio.
evidence: Based on genotyping data from breeding experiments.

claim: There is no difference in the brain/body weight ratio between Rem2-/- and Rem2+/+ littermates at P7, P21 or P30.
source: We found no difference in the brain/body weight ratio between Rem2-/- and Rem2+/+ (i.e. wildtype) littermates at P7, P21 or P30 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by brain/body weight measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is no significant change in cortical thickness at P7 and P21 between wildtype and Rem2-/- mice.
source: While we found no significant change in cortical thickness at P7 and P21, we did observe a small increase in cortical thickness at P30 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, p=0.05).
evidence: Supported by cortical thickness measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A small increase in cortical thickness at P30 was observed in Rem2-/- mice compared to wildtype.
source: While we found no significant change in cortical thickness at P7 and P21, we did observe a small increase in cortical thickness at P30 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, p=0.05).
evidence: Supported by cortical thickness measurements at P30 showing statistical significance (p=0.05) in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Layer thickness was indistinguishable between Rem2-/- and wildtype mice at P16.
source: We also examined cortical layer thickness by Nissl staining 30 μm sections through the visual cortex at P16 and found that layer thickness was indistinguishable between Rem2-/- and wildtype mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by Nissl staining and layer thickness measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Cortical development at the gross anatomical level proceeds relatively normally despite the absence of Rem2.
source: Thus, we conclude that cortical development at the gross anatomical level proceeds relatively normally despite the absence of Rem2.
evidence: Based on the lack of major differences in brain weight, cortical thickness, and layer organization between wildtype and Rem2-/- mice.

claim: There is no difference in the resting Ca2+ levels of cortical neurons obtained from wildtype, Rem2+/-, or Rem2-/- mice.
source: Interestingly, we found no difference in the resting Ca2+ levels of cortical neurons obtained from wildtype, Rem2+/-, or Rem2-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data showing similar resting calcium ratios across genotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Endogenous Rem2 does not alter the Ca2+ permeability at rest in young cortical neurons, or compensatory mechanisms exist to maintain normal resting calcium levels in the absence of Rem2 expression.
source: These data suggest that either endogenous Rem2 does not alter the Ca2+ permeability at rest in young cortical neurons, or that in the absence of Rem2 expression, compensatory mechanisms exist to maintain normal resting calcium levels.
evidence: Based on the observation of similar resting calcium levels across genotypes.

claim: No differences in measures of orientation tuning (circular variance) were observed between wildtype and Rem2-/- neurons.
source: No differences in measures of orientation tuning (circular variance, (Ringach et al., 2002), or in measures of direction selectivity (circular variance in direction space, (Mazurek et al., 2014) were observed between wildtype and Rem2-/- neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H,I), indicating that basic visual response tuning properties are normal in Rem2-/- mice.
evidence: Supported by two-photon calcium imaging data showing similar orientation selectivity between genotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).

claim: No differences in measures of direction selectivity were observed between wildtype and Rem2-/- neurons.
source: No differences in measures of orientation tuning (circular variance, (Ringach et al., 2002), or in measures of direction selectivity (circular variance in direction space, (Mazurek et al., 2014) were observed between wildtype and Rem2-/- neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H,I), indicating that basic visual response tuning properties are normal in Rem2-/- mice.
evidence: Supported by two-photon calcium imaging data showing similar direction selectivity between genotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).

claim: Basic visual response tuning properties are normal in Rem2-/- mice.
source: No differences in measures of orientation tuning (circular variance, (Ringach et al., 2002), or in measures of direction selectivity (circular variance in direction space, (Mazurek et al., 2014) were observed between wildtype and Rem2-/- neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H,I), indicating that basic visual response tuning properties are normal in Rem2-/- mice.
evidence: Based on the lack of differences in orientation and direction selectivity measurements.

claim: Deletion of Rem2 does not interfere substantially with initial brain or circuit development in the embryonic or early postnatal period of mouse development.
source: Taken together, our data suggests that, despite the expression of Rem2 during this developmental window, deletion of Rem2 does not interfere substantially with initial brain or circuit development in the embryonic or early postnatal period of mouse development.
evidence: Based on the collective observations of normal brain anatomy, cortical structure, resting calcium levels, and visual tuning properties.

claim: In wildtype mice, visual experience resulted in a significant increase in spine density relative to dark-reared animals.
source: In wildtype mice, visual experience resulted in a significant increase in spine density relative to dark-reared animals, similar to previous reports (Figure 2—figure supplement 2: WT LR = 0.98 ± 0.01 spines/μm; WT DR = 0.83 ± 0.01 spines/μm, p=0.00012; (Valverde, 1971; Wallace and Bear, 2004).
evidence: Supported by Golgi-Cox spine density measurements comparing light-reared and dark-reared wildtype mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Rem2-/- mice did not exhibit an experience-dependent increase in spine density.
source: However, Rem2-/- mice did not exhibit an experience-dependent increase in spine density (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Rem2-/- DR = 0.87 ± 0.01 spines/μm, p=0.58 compared to Rem2-/- LR).
evidence: Supported by Golgi-Cox spine density measurements showing no significant difference between light-reared and dark-reared Rem2-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Rem2 functions to promote experience-dependent synapse formation in vivo.
source: Consistent with our previous in vitro experiments, these results suggest that Rem2 functions to promote experience-dependent synapse formation in vivo.
evidence: Based on the lack of experience-dependent spine density increase in Rem2-/- mice compared to wildtype.

claim: Wildtype typically-reared littermate controls exhibited normal OD plasticity.
source: Wildtype typically-reared littermate controls exhibited normal OD plasticity (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging data showing expected shifts in ODI following monocular deprivation (Figure 3C).

claim: Closure of the contralateral eye for 2 days (P26-28) produced an initial, significant shift in the ODI in wildtype mice.
source: Closure of the contralateral eye for 2 days (P26-28) produced an initial, significant shift in the ODI (Figure 3C, WT TR = 0.35 ± 0.03 ODI; WT 2d MD = 0.15 ± 0.04 ODI, p=0.006).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements showing ODI shift after 2 days of monocular deprivation (Figure 3C).

claim: Prolonged MD for 6 days (P26-32) resulted in a further robust shift in OD toward the ipsilateral eye in wildtype mice.
source: In a separate experimental group, prolonged MD for 6 days (P26-32) resulted in a further robust shift in OD toward the ipsilateral eye (Figure 3C, WT 6d MD = −0.11 ± 0.04 ODI, p=0.000001 compared to WT TR) as has been previously reported (Gordon and Stryker, 1996; Heimel et al., 2007; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements showing further ODI shift after 6 days of monocular deprivation (Figure 3C).

claim: Responses to the contralateral (deprived) eye were decreased during the early-phase of deprivation (2d MD) in wildtype mice.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Gordon and Stryker, 1996; Heimel et al., 2007; Kaneko et al., 2008b; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007), responses to the contralateral (deprived) eye were decreased during the early-phase of deprivation (2d MD), while responses to the ipsilateral eye increased slightly during the late-phase of deprivation (6d MD; Figure 3C, inset, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by individual eye response measurements (ΔR/R) shown in Figure 3C inset and Table 1.

claim: Responses to the ipsilateral eye increased slightly during the late-phase of deprivation (6d MD) in wildtype mice.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Gordon and Stryker, 1996; Heimel et al., 2007; Kaneko et al., 2008b; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007), responses to the contralateral (deprived) eye were decreased during the early-phase of deprivation (2d MD), while responses to the ipsilateral eye increased slightly during the late-phase of deprivation (6d MD; Figure 3C, inset, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by individual eye response measurements (ΔR/R) shown in Figure 3C inset and Table 1.

claim: Rem2-/- mice with normal visual experience (Rem2-/- TR) displayed an ODI similar to that observed in wildtype mice.
source: Rem2-/- mice with normal visual experience (Rem2-/- TR) displayed an ODI similar to that observed in wildtype mice (Figure 3C, Rem2-/- TR = 0.35 ± 0.06 ODI, p=0.54 compared to WT TR).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements showing similar baseline ODI between genotypes (Figure 3C).

claim: Closure of the contralateral eye in Rem2-/- mice for 2 days induced an initial, significant shift in the ODI similar to that observed in WT mice.
source: Closure of the contralateral eye in Rem2-/- mice for 2 days induced an initial, significant shift in the ODI similar to that observed in WT mice (Figure 3C, Rem2-/- 2d MD = 0.17 ± 0.03 ODI, p=0.008), indicating that early-phase OD plasticity is intact in the absence of Rem2.
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements showing ODI shift after 2 days MD in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 3C).

claim: Early-phase OD plasticity is intact in the absence of Rem2.
source: Closure of the contralateral eye in Rem2-/- mice for 2 days induced an initial, significant shift in the ODI similar to that observed in WT mice (Figure 3C, Rem2-/- 2d MD = 0.17 ± 0.03 ODI, p=0.008), indicating that early-phase OD plasticity is intact in the absence of Rem2.
evidence: Based on the similar ODI shift observed in both wildtype and Rem2-/- mice after 2 days of monocular deprivation.

claim: The magnitude of depression of the deprived, contralateral eye responses following 2d MD in Rem2-/- mice is similar to those observed in wildtype mice.
source: As expected, the magnitude of depression of the deprived, contralateral eye responses following 2d MD in Rem2-/- mice is similar to those observed in wildtype mice (Figure 3C, inset 2d MD, Table 1), and suggests that a weakening of synaptic strength, reminiscent of LTD, is indeed induced in either the presence or absence of Rem2.
evidence: Supported by individual eye response measurements (ΔR/R) shown in Figure 3C inset and Table 1.

claim: A weakening of synaptic strength, reminiscent of LTD, is induced in either the presence or absence of Rem2 following 2d MD.
source: As expected, the magnitude of depression of the deprived, contralateral eye responses following 2d MD in Rem2-/- mice is similar to those observed in wildtype mice (Figure 3C, inset 2d MD, Table 1), and suggests that a weakening of synaptic strength, reminiscent of LTD, is indeed induced in either the presence or absence of Rem2.
evidence: Based on the similar decrease in contralateral eye responses in both genotypes after 2d MD.

claim: Late-phase OD plasticity was altered in Rem2-/- mice relative to their WT littermate controls.
source: However, in contrast to early phase plasticity, late-phase OD plasticity was altered in Rem2-/- mice relative to their WT littermate controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements showing different ODI outcomes after 6 days MD between genotypes (Figure 3C).

claim: Following 6 days of MD, Rem2-/- mice failed to display a further shift in ODI.
source: Following 6 days of MD, Rem2-/- mice failed to display a further shift in ODI (Figure 3C, Rem2-/- 6d MD = 0.10 ± 0.02 ODI vs. WT 6d MD −0.11 ± 0.04 ODI, p=0.0008 vs. Rem2-/- 2d MD = 0.17 ± 0.03, p=0.44), indicating a deficit in late-phase OD plasticity.
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements showing lack of further ODI shift in Rem2-/- mice between 2d and 6d MD (Figure 3C).

claim: Rem2-/- mice exhibit a deficit in late-phase OD plasticity.
source: Following 6 days of MD, Rem2-/- mice failed to display a further shift in ODI (Figure 3C, Rem2-/- 6d MD = 0.10 ± 0.02 ODI vs. WT 6d MD −0.11 ± 0.04 ODI, p=0.0008 vs. Rem2-/- 2d MD = 0.17 ± 0.03, p=0.44), indicating a deficit in late-phase OD plasticity.
evidence: Based on the lack of further ODI shift in Rem2-/- mice after 6 days MD compared to wildtype.

claim: Both WT and Rem2-/- mice exhibited a decrease in responses to the contralateral (deprived) eye after 2d MD.
source: Both WT and Rem2-/- mice exhibited a decrease in responses to the contralateral (deprived) eye after 2d MD (Figure 3C, inset).
evidence: Supported by individual eye response measurements (ΔR/R) shown in Figure 3C inset.

claim: Upon 6d of MD, WT mice exhibited an increase in ipsilateral (open) eye response.
source: However, upon 6d of MD, WT mice exhibited an increase in ipsilateral (open) eye response (Figure 3C, inset WT 6d MD).
evidence: Supported by individual eye response measurements (ΔR/R) shown in Figure 3C inset.

claim: The increased ipsilateral eye response in WT mice at 6d MD has been previously attributed to homeostatic mechanisms.
source: This increased response has been previously attributed to homeostatic mechanisms (Kaneko et al., 2008b; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013), which presumably interact with continued reductions in responses to the contralateral eye to promote a further shift in ODI.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating homeostatic mechanisms in OD plasticity.

claim: Rem2-/- mice exhibited relatively equal increases in both the contralateral eye and ipsilateral eye responses with 6d MD.
source: By contrast, Rem2-/- mice exhibited relatively equal increases in both the contralateral eye and ipsilateral eye responses with 6d MD.
evidence: Supported by individual eye response measurements (ΔR/R) shown in Figure 3C inset.

claim: Rem2-/- animals exhibited a non-competitive increase in activity during late-phase MD.
source: Thus, Rem2-/- animals exhibited a non-competitive increase in activity during late-phase MD.
evidence: Based on the observation of increased responses to both eyes in Rem2-/- mice at 6d MD.

claim: Rem2 may play an important role in regulating the absolute responsiveness of the cortex to visual stimulation, such as through regulation of neuronal excitability or synaptic scaling.
source: These results raise the possibility that Rem2 may play an important role in regulating the absolute responsiveness of the cortex to visual stimulation, such as through regulation of neuronal excitability or synaptic scaling.
evidence: Based on the non-competitive increase in visual responses observed in Rem2-/- mice.

claim: Wildtype mice monocularly deprived for 7–10 days in adulthood produced a robust shift in ODI from a contralateral bias to an ipsilateral bias.
source: Wildtype mice monocularly deprived for 7–10 days in adulthood produced a robust shift in ODI from a contralateral bias to an ipsilateral bias (Figure 3D, Adult WT TR = 0.30 ± 0.04 ODI; Adult WT MD = −0.15 ± 0.12 ODI, p=0.0005).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements in adult wildtype mice (Figure 3D).

claim: Rem2-/- mice that underwent monocular deprivation in adulthood also produced a significant shift in ODI following 7–10 days of MD.
source: Similarly, Rem2-/- mice that underwent monocular deprivation in adulthood also produced a significant shift in ODI following 7–10 days of MD (Figure 3D, Adult Rem2-/- TR = 0.37 ± 0.07 ODI; Adult Rem2-/- MD = −0.05 ± 0.09 ODI, p=0.003).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements in adult Rem2-/- mice (Figure 3D).

claim: Rem2 is required specifically for late-phase critical period plasticity.
source: Thus, taken together these data suggest that Rem2 is required specifically for late-phase critical period plasticity.
evidence: Based on the observation that Rem2-/- mice show normal early-phase critical period plasticity and normal adult plasticity, but impaired late-phase critical period plasticity.

claim: The Rem2+/+; Emx1Cre mice showed a pronounced shift in their ODI following 5–7 days of MD.
source: The Rem2+/+; Emx1Cre mice showed a pronounced shift in their ODI following 5–7 days of MD as expected (Figure 4A, Rem2+/+; Emx1Cre TR = 0.33 ± 0.06 ODI; Rem2+/+; Emx1Cre MD = −0.06 ± 0.06 ODI, p=0.0005).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements in Rem2+/+; Emx1Cre control mice (Figure 4A).

claim: Rem2 deletion specifically from excitatory, cortical neurons (Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre) resulted in diminished OD plasticity following MD.
source: However, Rem2 deletion specifically from excitatory, cortical neurons (Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre) resulted in diminished OD plasticity following MD (Figure 4A, Rem2 flx/flx; Emx1Cre TR = 0. 31 ± 0.04 ODI; Rem2 flx/flx; Emx1Cre MD = 0.21 ± 0.06 ODI, p=0.61).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements in Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre mice (Figure 4A).

claim: Rem2 is required in the cortex to mediate proper OD plasticity.
source: We made two important conclusions based on this data. First, Rem2 is required in the cortex to mediate proper OD plasticity, as the Emx1 promoter does not drive Cre expression in other upstream regions of the visual system such as thalamus and retina (Gorski et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on the OD plasticity deficit observed in Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre mice and the known expression pattern of Emx1-Cre.

claim: Within the cortex, Rem2 is required in excitatory glutamatergic neurons for critical period ocular dominance plasticity to occur.
source: Second, within the cortex, Rem2 is required in excitatory glutamatergic neurons for critical period ocular dominance plasticity to occur.
evidence: Based on the OD plasticity deficit observed when Rem2 is deleted from excitatory neurons using Emx1-Cre.

claim: A significant shift in the ODI was observed in Rem2+/+; PvalbCre mice following monocular deprivation.
source: As expected, we observed a significant shift in the ODI in Rem2+/+; PvalbCre mice following monocular deprivation (Figure 4B, Rem2+/+; PvalbCre TR = 0.30 ± 0.04 ODI; Rem2+/+; PvalbCre MD = −0.05 ± 0.06 ODI, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements in Rem2+/+; PvalbCre control mice (Figure 4B).

claim: Deletion of Rem2 from Pvalb+ interneurons (Rem2flx/flx; PvalbCre) had no effect on OD plasticity.
source: However, in contrast to the lack of OD plasticity observed in the Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre mice, deletion of Rem2 from Pvalb+ interneurons (Rem2flx/flx; PvalbCre) had no effect on OD plasticity (Figure 4B, Rem2flx/flx; PvalbCre TR = 0.34 ± 0.05 ODI, Rem2flx/flx; PvalbCre MD = −0.01 ± 0.07 ODI, p=0.0005).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements in Rem2flx/flx; PvalbCre mice showing normal OD plasticity (Figure 4B).

claim: Rem2 is not required in Pvalb+ interneurons for OD plasticity.
source: These data demonstrate that Rem2 is not required in Pvalb+ interneurons for OD plasticity.
evidence: Based on the normal OD plasticity observed in Rem2flx/flx; PvalbCre mice.

claim: A significant shift in the ODI was observed in Rem2+/+; VipCre mice following monocular deprivation.
source: We observed a significant shift in the ODI in Rem2+/+; VipCre mice following monocular deprivation (Figure 4C, Rem2+/+; VipCre TR = 0.39 ± 0.01 ODI; Rem2+/+; VipCre MD = 0.04 ± 0.02 ODI, p=0.01).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements in Rem2+/+; VipCre control mice (Figure 4C).

claim: Deletion of Rem2 from Vip+ interneurons has no effect on OD plasticity.
source: A similar shift was observed in the monocularly deprived Rem2flx/flx; VipCre mice, indicating that deletion of Rem2 from Vip+ interneurons has no effect on OD plasticity (Figure 4C, Rem2flx/flx; VipCre TR = 0.32 ± 0.03 ODI; Rem2flx/flx; VipCre MD = −0.00 ± 0.09 ODI, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by intrinsic signal imaging measurements in Rem2flx/flx; VipCre mice showing normal OD plasticity (Figure 4C).

claim: Rem2 is not required in either Pvalb+ or Vip+ interneurons for critical period OD plasticity.
source: Taken together these data demonstrate that Rem2 is not required in either Pvalb+ or Vip+ interneurons for critical period OD plasticity.
evidence: Based on the normal OD plasticity observed in both Rem2flx/flx; PvalbCre and Rem2flx/flx; VipCre mice.

claim: The Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre animals exhibit a smaller shift in ocular dominance after 6d MD than the Rem2-/- animals when compared to their respective littermate controls.
source: Interestingly, the Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre animals exhibit a smaller shift in ocular dominance after 6d MD than the Rem2-/- animals when compared to their respective littermate controls (compare Figure 3C to Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of ODI measurements between Rem2-/- (Figure 3C) and Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre (Figure 4A) mice.

claim: Rem2 may modulate plasticity via its expression in different cell types or brain regions other than those examined by use of these particular Cre driver lines.
source: One possible explanation for this result is that Rem2 modulates plasticity via its expression in different cell types or brain regions other than those examined by use of these particular Cre driver lines in the current study.
evidence: Based on the difference in OD plasticity phenotype between Rem2-/- and Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre mice.

claim: Rem2 may function in other cell types, such as Vip+ interneurons, to help disinhibit cortical circuits and indirectly contribute to the partial shift observed in the Rem2-/- animals.
source: Thus, another possibility is that Rem2 may also function in other cell types, such as Vip+ interneurons, to help disinhibit cortical circuits and indirectly contribute to the partial shift observed in the Rem2-/- animals that is absent in the Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre mice.
evidence: Based on previous work showing Igf1 in Vip+ interneurons affects inhibitory tone but not OD plasticity, and the difference in phenotype between Rem2-/- and Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre mice.

claim: 2 days of monocular deprivation in wildtype mice resulted in a significant decrease in mEPSC amplitude recorded from layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We found that 2 days of monocular deprivation in wildtype mice resulted in a significant decrease in mEPSC amplitude recorded from layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 5A,C and E (left); WT TR = −9.8 ± 0.1 pA; WT 2d MD = −8.87 ± 0.08 pA, p=0.015) as previously reported (Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mEPSCs showing decreased amplitude after 2d MD (Figure 5A,C,E).

claim: Recordings from layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in cortical slices obtained from Rem2-/- mice following 2 days of MD resulted in a significant decrease in mEPSC amplitude.
source: Similarly, recordings from layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in cortical slices obtained from Rem2-/- mice following 2 days of MD also resulted in a significant decrease in mEPSC amplitude (Figure 5A,C and E (left), Rem2-/- P28 TR = −9.76 ± 0.08 pA; Rem2-/- 2d MD = −9.12 ± 0.08 pA, p=0.014).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mEPSCs showing decreased amplitude after 2d MD in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 5A,C,E).

claim: In the absence of Rem2, layer 2/3 cortical neurons are sensitive to the decrease in drive that occurs as a result of MD and decrease their excitatory postsynaptic strength.
source: These data, in agreement with our 2d MD ODI data in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 3C), suggest that in the absence of Rem2, layer 2/3 cortical neurons are sensitive to the decrease in drive that occurs as a result of MD and decrease their excitatory postsynaptic strength as expected (Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013).
evidence: Based on the observed decrease in mEPSC amplitude in Rem2-/- mice after 2d MD, consistent with ODI data.

claim: A significant increase in mEPSC amplitude was found in neurons in slices obtained from wildtype animals following 6 days of MD.
source: As expected, we found a significant increase in mEPSC amplitude in neurons in slices obtained from wildtype animals following 6 days of MD (Figure 5B,C and E (right); WT TR = −9.46 ± 0.1 pA; WT 6d MD = −10.31 ± 0.09 pA, p=0.027).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mEPSCs showing increased amplitude after 6d MD (Figure 5B,C,E).

claim: The magnitude of the mEPSC amplitude increase following 6d MD (~10% increase) is consistent with previous reports.
source: The magnitude of the effect (~10% increase following 6d MD) is consistent with previous reports (Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work showing similar magnitude of synaptic scaling.

claim: No significant increase in mEPSC amplitude was observed in neurons from Rem2-/- visual cortex following 6 days of MD.
source: However, we failed to observe a significant increase in mEPSC amplitude in neurons from Rem2-/- visual cortex following 6 days of MD (Figure 5B,C and E (right); Rem2-/- TR = −9.64 ± 0.12 pA; Rem2-/- 6d MD = −9.04 ± 0.14 pA, p=0.535).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mEPSCs showing no change in amplitude after 6d MD in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 5B,C,E).

claim: Excitatory postsynaptic scaling up is aberrant in Rem2-/- mice.
source: Thus, these data demonstrate that excitatory postsynaptic scaling up is aberrant in Rem2-/- mice.
evidence: Based on the lack of mEPSC amplitude increase in Rem2-/- mice after 6d MD.

claim: No change in mEPSC frequency was found in wildtype mice following either 2 days or 6 days of MD.
source: As expected, we found no change in mEPSC frequency in wildtype mice following either 2 days (Figure 5D,F (left); WT TR = 4.69 ± 0.13 Hz; WT 2d MD = 4.12 ± 0.1 Hz, p=0.515) or 6 days of MD (Figure 5D,F (right); WT TR = 3.65 ± 0.13 Hz; WT 6d MD = 3.95 ± 0.1 Hz, p=0.551).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mEPSCs showing no change in frequency after MD (Figure 5D,F).

claim: Both P28 and P32 typically reared Rem2-/- mice displayed a significant decrease in mEPSC frequency when compared to their wildtype littermate controls reared under the same conditions.
source: Interestingly, both P28 and P32 typically reared Rem2-/- mice displayed a significant decrease in mEPSC frequency when compared to their wildtype littermate controls reared under the same conditions (Figure 5D,F; Rem2-/- P28 TR = 4.13 ± 0.1 Hz, p=0.03; Rem2-/- P32 TR = −2.34 ± 0.1 Hz, p=0.0005).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mEPSCs showing decreased frequency in Rem2-/- mice at baseline (Figure 5D,F).

claim: The frequency of mEPSC events was further decreased following both 2 days and 6 days of MD in cortical neurons isolated from Rem2-/- compared to wildtype animals.
source: The frequency of mEPSC events was still further decreased following both 2 days (Figure 5E,F (left); Rem2-/- 2d MD = 3.19 ± 0.12 Hz, p=0.003) and 6 days of MD (Figure 5E,F (right); Rem2-/- 6d MD = 1.6 ± 0.05 Hz, p=0.008) in cortical neurons isolated from Rem2-/- compared to wildtype animals.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mEPSCs showing further decreased frequency after MD in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 5D,F).

claim: Changes in mEPSC frequency in Rem2-/- mice could reflect differences in excitatory synapse formation, presynaptic neurotransmitter release, or synapse maintenance and pruning mechanisms.
source: These changes in mEPSC frequency could reflect any number of differences between the cortical synaptic connections in the Rem2-/- and wildtype mice in the context of sensory deprivation including changes in excitatory synapse formation, presynaptic neurotransmitter release, or synapse maintenance and pruning mechanisms.
evidence: Based on the observed changes in mEPSC frequency in Rem2-/- mice.

claim: No change in mIPSC frequency or amplitude was found in response to 6 days of MD in wildtype neurons.
source: We found no change in mIPSC frequency (Figure 6A,B; WT TR = 5.63 ± 0.09 Hz; WT 6d MD = 5.31 ± 0.13 Hz, p=0.931) or amplitude (Figure 6C,D; WT TR = −31.04 ± 1.0 pA; WT 6d MD = −31.92 ± 0.92 pA, p=0.852) in response to 6 days of MD in wildtype neurons.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mIPSCs showing no change after 6d MD in wildtype mice (Figure 6).

claim: mIPSC frequency and amplitude recorded from neurons in Rem2-/- mice that were typically reared was similar to WT TR neurons.
source: Additionally, mIPSC frequency and amplitude recorded from neurons in Rem2-/- mice that were typically reared was similar to WT TR neurons, suggesting that deletion of Rem2 does not alter baseline inhibitory synapse formation or transmission (Figure 6, (B) Rem2-/- TR frequency = 5.27 ± 0.13 Hz; (C, D) amplitude = −29.22 ± 1.47 pA, p=0.73 compared to WT TR).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mIPSCs showing similar baseline values between genotypes (Figure 6).

claim: Deletion of Rem2 does not alter baseline inhibitory synapse formation or transmission.
source: Additionally, mIPSC frequency and amplitude recorded from neurons in Rem2-/- mice that were typically reared was similar to WT TR neurons, suggesting that deletion of Rem2 does not alter baseline inhibitory synapse formation or transmission (Figure 6, (B) Rem2-/- TR frequency = 5.27 ± 0.13 Hz; (C, D) amplitude = −29.22 ± 1.47 pA, p=0.73 compared to WT TR).
evidence: Based on the similar mIPSC frequency and amplitude between wildtype and Rem2-/- typically reared mice.

claim: A significant increase in mIPSC frequency, but not amplitude, was observed in Rem2-/- mice with 6 days of MD.
source: We did, however, observe a significant increase in mIPSC frequency, but not amplitude, in Rem2-/- mice with 6 days of MD (Figure 6B–D, Rem2-/- 6d MD frequency = 6.32 ± 0.13 Hz, p=0.03; Rem2-/- 6d MD amplitude = −29.02 ± 1.0 pA, p=0.35 compared to Rem2-/- TR).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mIPSCs showing increased frequency after 6d MD in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 6).

claim: The increase in mIPSC frequency with 6d MD observed in layer 2/3 neurons obtained from Rem2-/- mice is concurrent with a decrease in mEPSC frequency at the same experimental time point, suggesting that a change in network excitability has occurred.
source: Interestingly, the increase in mIPSC frequency with 6d MD observed in layer 2/3 neurons obtained from Rem2-/- mice is concurrent with a decrease in mEPSC frequency at the same experimental time point (Figure 5D), suggesting that a change in network excitability has occurred.
evidence: Based on the concurrent changes in mIPSC and mEPSC frequency in Rem2-/- mice at 6d MD.

claim: Rem2-/- mice exhibited a pronounced leftward shift of the f-I curve under normal rearing conditions.
source: Surprisingly, Rem2-/- mice exhibited a pronounced leftward shift of the f-I curve under normal rearing conditions (Figure 7), suggesting that Rem2 normally functions to inhibit the intrinsic excitability of the neuron.
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing increased firing rate in response to current injection in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 7).

claim: Rem2 normally functions to inhibit the intrinsic excitability of the neuron.
source: Surprisingly, Rem2-/- mice exhibited a pronounced leftward shift of the f-I curve under normal rearing conditions (Figure 7), suggesting that Rem2 normally functions to inhibit the intrinsic excitability of the neuron.
evidence: Based on the increased intrinsic excitability observed in Rem2-/- mice at baseline.

claim: The shift in f-I curve in Rem2-/- mice occurred in the absence of changes in RIN, Vm or Cm between wildtype and Rem2-/- neurons.
source: This shift occurred in the absence of changes in RIN, Vm or Cm (Table 2) between wildtype and Rem2-/- neurons (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by passive membrane property measurements showing no differences in RIN, Vm, or Cm (Table 2).

claim: Following 2 days of MD, wildtype neurons displayed no change in their f-I curve.
source: Following 2 days of MD, wildtype neurons displayed no change in their f-I curve (Figure 7A–B, compare WT TR to WT 2d MD), while Rem2-/- neurons displayed decreased firing (Figure 7A–B, compare Rem2-/- TR to Rem2-/- 2d MD), such that the f-I curves obtained from Rem2-/- neurons were indistinguishable from wildtype (Figure 7B, compare Rem2-/- 2d MD to WT TR).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing no change in f-I curve in wildtype mice after 2d MD (Figure 7A-B).

claim: Rem2-/- neurons displayed decreased firing following 2 days of MD, such that the f-I curves obtained from Rem2-/- neurons were indistinguishable from wildtype.
source: Following 2 days of MD, wildtype neurons displayed no change in their f-I curve (Figure 7A–B, compare WT TR to WT 2d MD), while Rem2-/- neurons displayed decreased firing (Figure 7A–B, compare Rem2-/- TR to Rem2-/- 2d MD), such that the f-I curves obtained from Rem2-/- neurons were indistinguishable from wildtype (Figure 7B, compare Rem2-/- 2d MD to WT TR).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing decreased firing in Rem2-/- mice after 2d MD (Figure 7A-B).

claim: When examined after 6 days of MD, wildtype neurons shifted their f-I curve to the left, indicating a homeostatic increase in intrinsic excitability.
source: In contrast, when examined after 6 days of MD, wildtype neurons shifted their f-I curve to the left (Figure 7C–D, compare WT TR to WT 6d MD), indicating a homeostatic increase in intrinsic excitability (Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing leftward shift in f-I curve in wildtype mice after 6d MD (Figure 7C-D).

claim: Neurons from Rem2-/- mice failed to further increase their intrinsic excitability in response to 6 days of MD.
source: However, neurons from Rem2-/- mice failed to further increase their intrinsic excitability in response to 6 days of MD (Figure 7D, compare Rem2-/- TR to Rem2-/- 6d MD).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing no further change in f-I curve in Rem2-/- mice after 6d MD (Figure 7D).

claim: Rem2 normally functions to stabilize intrinsic excitability, as removal of Rem2 causes increased intrinsic excitability.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Rem2 normally functions to stabilize intrinsic excitability, as removal of Rem2 causes increased intrinsic excitability (Figure 7, TR Rem2-/-).
evidence: Based on the increased baseline intrinsic excitability in Rem2-/- mice.

claim: Short and long-term deprivation (2d vs. 6d MD), in the presence or absence of Rem2, has different effects on intrinsic excitability.
source: However, short and long-term deprivation (2d vs. 6d MD), in the presence or absence of Rem2, has different effects on intrinsic excitability (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by the different patterns of f-I curve changes observed at 2d versus 6d MD in both genotypes (Figure 7).

claim: Other signaling pathways, in addition to Rem2, function to regulate intrinsic excitability in the context of sensory deprivation and are responsive to the amount of deprivation that has occurred.
source: These data imply the existence of other signaling pathways, in addition to Rem2, which also function to regulate intrinsic excitability in the context of sensory deprivation and further, are responsive to the amount of deprivation that has occurred.
evidence: Based on the different effects of 2d versus 6d MD on intrinsic excitability in both wildtype and Rem2-/- mice.

claim: Acute, sparse deletion of Rem2 from layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons 4 d.p.i. led to a significant increase in intrinsic excitability in response to current injection.
source: Surprisingly, we found that acute, sparse deletion of Rem2 from layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons 4 d.p.i. led to a significant increase in intrinsic excitability in response to current injection (Figure 8B, Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre 4 d.p.i.) compared to those with normal Rem2 expression (Figure 8B, Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP 4 d.p.i.).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing increased firing in Rem2-deleted neurons at 4 d.p.i. (Figure 8B).

claim: Deletion of Rem2 for 10–12 d.p.i. resulted in a significant increase in intrinsic excitability.
source: Similarly, deletion of Rem2 for 10–12 d.p.i. also resulted in a significant increase in intrinsic excitability (Figure 8C, Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre 10–12 d.p.i.) compared to their wildtype littermate controls (Figure 8C, Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP 10–12 d.p.i.).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing increased firing in Rem2-deleted neurons at 10-12 d.p.i. (Figure 8C).

claim: A primary function of Rem2 is to regulate intrinsic excitability in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: These results indicate that a primary function of Rem2 is to regulate intrinsic excitability in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: Based on the increased intrinsic excitability observed following sparse, acute deletion of Rem2.

claim: Acute deletion of Rem2 measured 4 d.p.i. did not alter mEPSC frequency or amplitude.
source: Interestingly, we found that acute deletion of Rem2 measured 4 d.p.i. did not alter mEPSC frequency or amplitude (Figure 8D, (left) frequency: Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP=5.59 ± 0.22 Hz; Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre=5.10 ± 0.24 Hz, p=0.423; (right) amplitude: Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP=−10.28 ± 0.31 pA; Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre=−9.60 ± 0.24 pA, p=0.386).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mEPSCs showing no change at 4 d.p.i. (Figure 8D).

claim: By 10–12 d.p.i. a significant decrease in mEPSC frequency with no change in mEPSC amplitude was observed following Rem2 deletion.
source: Conversely, by 10–12 d.p.i. a significant decrease in mEPSC frequency (Figure 8E, left; Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP=4.38 ± 0.15 Hz; Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre=2.92 ± 0.19 Hz, p=0.011) with no change in mEPSC amplitude was observed (Figure 8E right; Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP=−9.76 ± 0.22 pA; Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre=−10.42 ± 0.26 Hz, p=0.38).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of mEPSCs showing decreased frequency at 10-12 d.p.i. (Figure 8E).

claim: Acute deletion of Rem2 (10 d.p.i.) resulted in decreased spine density and spine head width, as well as a statistically significant decrease in spine neck length.
source: Acute deletion of Rem2 (10 d.p.i.), resulted in decreased spine density and spine head width, as well as a statistically significant decrease in spine neck length (Fig. S3).
evidence: Supported by spine morphology measurements in Rem2-deleted neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: Approximately 10 days following Rem2 deletion there is a significant decrease in functional synapses, prior to spine shrinkage and eventual removal.
source: These results, together with our mEPSC data (Figure 8D–E), suggest that approximately 10 days following Rem2 deletion there is a significant decrease in functional synapses, prior to spine shrinkage and eventual removal.
evidence: Based on the temporal sequence of changes in mEPSC frequency and spine morphology following Rem2 deletion.

claim: Rem2 functions in a cell-autonomous manner to regulate intrinsic excitability irrespective of changes in excitatory synaptic density.
source: Therefore, we conclude that Rem2 functions in a cell-autonomous manner to regulate intrinsic excitability irrespective of changes in excitatory synaptic density.
evidence: Based on the observation that increased intrinsic excitability occurs before changes in mEPSC frequency following Rem2 deletion.

claim: The dramatic decrease in mEPSC frequency observed in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in Rem2-/- mice most likely reflects a combination of both presynaptic and postsynaptic effects of Rem2 deletion.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the dramatic decrease in mEPSC frequency observed in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 5D, right) most likely reflects a combination of both presynaptic and postsynaptic effects of Rem2 deletion.
evidence: Based on the collective observations of changes in mEPSC frequency, spine density, and the temporal sequence of these changes.

claim: Deletion of Rem2 leads to a significant increase in spontaneous firing rates in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We found that deletion of Rem2 leads to a significant increase in spontaneous firing rates in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre=0.52 ± 0.067 Hz, p=0.008, Figure 9B top right) compared to wildtype control neurons (Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP=0.154 ± 0.029 Hz, Figure 9B top left).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings of spontaneous firing in Rem2-deleted neurons (Figure 9B).

claim: Rem2 functions cell-autonomously to stabilize neuronal firing rates.
source: Thus, Rem2 functions cell-autonomously to stabilize neuronal firing rates.
evidence: Based on the increased spontaneous firing rate observed following sparse deletion of Rem2.

claim: In both Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP and Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre mice, 2d MD had no effect on spontaneous firing rates recorded from GFP + layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In both Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP and Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre mice, 2d MD had no effect on spontaneous firing rates recorded from GFP + layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP 2d MD = 0.029 ± 0.0038 Hz, p=0.8442 compared to Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP; Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre 2d MD = 0.284 ± 0.0038 Hz, p=0.203 compared to Rem2flx/flx + AAV GFP-Cre).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings of spontaneous firing showing no change after 2d MD (Figure 9B,C).

claim: Decreased intrinsic excitability observed with 2d MD does not directly translate into changes in spontaneous firing rate in individual neurons.
source: These data suggest that decreased intrinsic excitability observed with 2d MD does not directly translate into changes in spontaneous firing rate in individual neurons (Figure 9C).
evidence: Based on the lack of change in spontaneous firing rate despite changes in intrinsic excitability at 2d MD.

claim: The decrease in intrinsic excitability observed in the Rem2-/- mouse following 2d MD may implicate additional roles for Rem2, such as regulating presynaptic neurotransmitter release.
source: Thus, it is possible that the decrease in intrinsic excitability observed in the Rem2-/- mouse following 2d MD (Figure 7A,B) implicates additional roles for Rem2. For example, Rem2 may play a role in regulating presynaptic neurotransmitter release, which in turn influences how individual neurons response to circuit-level changes in activity.
evidence: Based on the different experimental approaches (total knockout versus sparse knockout) and the observed phenotypes.

claim: No significant change in spontaneous firing rate was observed between wildtype and Rem2-/- mice at P28.
source: Interestingly, we observed no significant change in spontaneous firing rate between wildtype and Rem2-/- mice at P28 (Figure 10A–B, left).
evidence: Supported by in vivo extracellular recordings showing similar spontaneous firing rates at P28 (Figure 10A-B).

claim: A significant increase in spontaneous firing rate emerges at the P34 time point in Rem2-/- mice compared to wildtype.
source: However, a significant increase in spontaneous firing rate emerges at the P34 time point (Figure 10A–B, right).
evidence: Supported by in vivo extracellular recordings showing increased spontaneous firing rates at P34 in Rem2-/- mice (Figure 10A-B).

claim: In the absence of Rem2, the cortical network is more active.
source: Thus, in the absence of Rem2, the cortical network is more active.
evidence: Based on the increased spontaneous firing rate observed in vivo in Rem2-/- mice at P34.

claim: The increase in spontaneous firing rate recorded in vivo is consistent with the cell-autonomous increase in intrinsic excitability and spontaneous firing rates observed in ex vivo preparations.
source: In addition, the increase in spontaneous firing rate recorded in vivo is consistent with the cell-autonomous increase in intrinsic excitability and spontaneous firing rates observed in our ex vivo preparations.
evidence: Based on the concordance between in vivo and ex vivo observations of increased spontaneous firing in Rem2-/- mice.

claim: Rem2 regulates the absolute responsiveness of the cortex to visual stimulation through regulation of intrinsic excitability.
source: These data (Figures 7 and 9 and Figure 10) also provide a parsimonious explanation for the intrinsic signal imaging results observed in Rem2-/- animals (Figure 3C), and support the conclusion that Rem2 regulates the absolute responsiveness of the cortex to visual stimulation through regulation of intrinsic excitability.
evidence: Based on the collective observations of increased intrinsic excitability, spontaneous firing, and visual responsiveness in Rem2-/- mice.

claim: Rem2 normally functions to dampen intrinsic excitability during periods of robust activity.
source: Based on the data presented in this study, we favor a model in which Rem2 functions to dampen intrinsic excitability during periods of robust activity.
evidence: Based on the increased intrinsic excitability and spontaneous firing observed in the absence of Rem2.

claim: During periods of low activity, in which we expect little to no Rem2 expression, neurons alter their intrinsic excitability through other signaling pathways.
source: In this model, during periods of low activity, in which we expect little to no Rem2 expression, neurons alter their intrinsic excitability through other signaling pathways.
evidence: Based on the observed changes in intrinsic excitability with deprivation in both wildtype and Rem2-/- mice.

claim: Rem2 acts as a stabilizer to restrict excitability in high-activity regimes in order to maintain circuit function within an appropriate physiological range.
source: As such, we propose that Rem2 acts as a stabilizer to restrict excitability in high-activity regimes in order to maintain circuit function within an appropriate physiological range.
evidence: Based on the collective findings regarding Rem2's role in regulating intrinsic excitability and spontaneous firing.

claim: Rem2 functions in excitatory cortical neurons to mediate OD plasticity in response to long-term monocular deprivation during the critical period.
source: Our findings demonstrate that Rem2 functions in excitatory cortical neurons to mediate OD plasticity in response to long-term monocular deprivation during the critical period (Figures 3 and 4) in part through regulating intrinsic excitability and synaptic function.
evidence: Based on the OD plasticity deficits observed in Rem2-/- and Rem2flx/flx; Emx1Cre mice, and the cellular phenotypes observed.

claim: The activity-regulated gene Rem2 is required for homeostatic synaptic scaling up.
source: Consistent with this result, our electrophysiological studies demonstrate that the activity-regulated gene Rem2 is required for homeostatic synaptic scaling up (Figure 5) and proper regulation of intrinsic excitability in vivo (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on the lack of mEPSC amplitude increase in Rem2-/- mice after 6d MD.

claim: Rem2 may be required for proper homeostatic function during the critical period.
source: These data, combined with the observed deficit in late-phase OD plasticity (Figure 3C) and normal adult OD plasticity (Figure 3D) support the premise that Rem2 may be required for proper homeostatic function during the critical period.
evidence: Based on the pattern of OD plasticity deficits and cellular phenotypes observed in Rem2-/- mice.

claim: Rem2 may be a key molecule required for establishing and maintaining the firing rate set point during critical period development in vivo.
source: Further, we suggest the intriguing possibility that Rem2 may be a key molecule required for establishing and maintaining the firing rate set point during critical period development in vivo.
evidence: Based on Rem2's role in regulating intrinsic excitability and spontaneous firing rates.

claim: Impaired homeostatic scaling up in TNFα knockout mice results in a failure to increase open eye responsiveness, causing the observed deficit in OD plasticity.
source: For example, transgenic mice harboring a deletion of TNFα also display a deficit in late-phase OD plasticity (Kaneko et al., 2008b) and normal adult OD plasticity (Ranson et al., 2012). In this study, the authors demonstrate that impaired homeostatic scaling up results in a failure to increase open eye responsiveness, causing the observed deficit in OD plasticity (Kaneko et al., 2008b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on TNFα knockout mice.

claim: Rem2-/- mice display both impaired synaptic scaling up and altered intrinsic excitability, as well as a generalized increase of individual eye responses with 6d MD.
source: In contrast, Rem2-/- mice display both impaired synaptic scaling up (Figure 5) and altered intrinsic excitability (Figure 7), as well as a generalized increase of individual eye responses with 6d MD (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by the collective data from mEPSC recordings, f-I curves, and intrinsic signal imaging.

claim: The results in Rem2-/- mice are similar to those observed following binocular deprivation, which leads to increased cortical responsiveness to both eyes.
source: These latter results are similar to those observed following binocular deprivation, which leads to increased cortical responsiveness to both eyes (Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on binocular deprivation.

claim: It is the combination of impaired synaptic scaling and increased intrinsic excitability that leads to the observed increase in spontaneous firing rates in vivo in Rem2-/- mice.
source: While it may seem counterintuitive to observe impaired synaptic scaling and increased intrinsic excitability as we do in the cortex of Rem2-/- mice, it is apparently this combination of cellular phenotypes that lead to the observed increase in spontaneous firing rates observed in vivo.
evidence: Based on the collective observations of cellular and circuit-level phenotypes in Rem2-/- mice.

claim: The discovery of the role of Rem2 in regulating intrinsic excitability provides novel insight into the importance of neuronal regulation of intrinsic excitability to sculpting network output.
source: Thus, while it remains to be determined exactly how these two processes function synergistically to maintain proper circuit function, our discovery of the role of Rem2 in this process provides novel insight into the importance of neuronal regulation of intrinsic excitability to sculpting network output.
evidence: Based on the novel findings regarding Rem2's role in regulating intrinsic excitability and its impact on circuit function.

claim: Rem2 is a noncanonical Ras-like GTPase, expressed throughout the cell and is unlikely to be regulated by its nucleotide binding state.
source: Rem2 is a noncanonical Ras-like GTPase, expressed throughout the cell (Ghiretti and Paradis, 2011) and is unlikely to be regulated by its nucleotide binding state (Correll et al., 2008) in contrast to canonical Ras family members.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work characterizing Rem2.

claim: Rem2 has been shown to associate with VGCC subunits and CaMKII.
source: The mechanism by which Rem2 transduces signals is an open area of investigation, although it has been shown to associate with VGCC subunits (Chen et al., 2005; Finlin et al., 2006; Finlin et al., 2005; Pang et al., 2010) and CaMKII (Flynn et al., 2012; Royer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work showing Rem2 interactions.

claim: Rem2 functions in a CaMK signaling pathway to regulate dendritic complexity.
source: In addition, our previous studies demonstrated that Rem2 functions in a CaMK signaling pathway to regulate dendritic complexity (Ghiretti et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: CREB is a known output of CaMK signaling and has been implicated in regulation of dendritic morphology, synaptic scaling, and intrinsic excitability.
source: Interestingly, CREB is a known output of CaMK signaling and has also been implicated in regulation of dendritic morphology (Redmond et al., 2002), synaptic scaling (Ibata et al., 2008; Joseph and Turrigiano, 2017), and intrinsic excitability (Dong et al., 2006; Joseph and Turrigiano, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on CREB function.

claim: Neuronal intrinsic excitability is under transcriptional control.
source: In fact, two of these studies (Dong et al., 2006; Joseph and Turrigiano, 2017) strongly suggest that neuronal intrinsic excitability is under transcriptional control.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work demonstrating transcriptional regulation of intrinsic excitability.

claim: Rem2 functions as a calcium-sensitive cytoplasmic signal transduction molecule, conveying changes at the membrane into changes in gene expression in the nucleus to regulate intrinsic excitability.
source: We propose that Rem2 functions as a calcium-sensitive cytoplasmic signal transduction molecule, conveying changes at the membrane (e.g. Ca2+ influx) into changes in gene expression in the nucleus (e.g. CREB) to regulate intrinsic excitability.
evidence: Based on Rem2's properties and the known signaling pathways it participates in.

claim: The expression of a number of ion channels, important for establishing neuronal excitability, are regulated by Rem2 signaling in an activity-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with this model, we performed RNA-sequencing to identify downstream targets of Rem2 (Kenny et al., 2017). We found that the expression of a number of ion channels, important for establishing neuronal excitability, are regulated by Rem2 signaling in an activity-dependent manner (Kenny et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous RNA-sequencing work from the authors' lab.

claim: Rem2 is a novel inhibitor of CaMKII catalytic activity.
source: We also recently demonstrated that Rem2 is a novel inhibitor of CaMKII catalytic activity (Royer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work from the authors' lab.

claim: CaMKII has been shown to modulate calcium channel function to alter intrinsic excitability.
source: Interestingly, CaMKII has been shown to modulate calcium channel function to alter intrinsic excitability (Sahu et al., 2017; van Welie et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on CaMKII function.

claim: Rem2 signaling may regulate neuronal intrinsic excitability by controlling the composition or function of ion channels at the cell membrane.
source: Thus, Rem2 signaling may regulate neuronal intrinsic excitability by controlling the composition or function of ion channels at the cell membrane.
evidence: Based on the known interactions of Rem2 with ion channels and CaMKII, and the observed effects on intrinsic excitability.

claim: Rem2 is an important regulator of synapse formation and dendritic morphology in cultured neurons and Xenopus optic tectum.
source: Our previous findings revealed that Rem2 is also an important regulator of synapse formation and dendritic morphology in cultured neurons and Xenopus optic tectum (Ghiretti et al., 2013; Ghiretti et al., 2014; Ghiretti and Paradis, 2011; Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: Rem2 regulates dendritic spine morphology in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: The current study also demonstrates that Rem2 regulates dendritic spine morphology in a cell-autonomous manner (Fig. S3), as well as experience-dependent changes in spine density (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by spine morphology measurements following sparse Rem2 deletion (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: Other activity signaling pathways also co-regulate experience-dependent circuit plasticity and synapse development.
source: Similar to our findings with Rem2, other activity signaling pathways also co-regulate experience-dependent circuit plasticity and synapse development (Piochon et al., 2016; Titley et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on other activity-regulated molecules.

claim: cpg15 is an important regulator of synapse formation and dendritic complexity and is required during the critical period for normal OD plasticity.
source: For example, cpg15 has been shown to be an important regulator of synapse formation and dendritic complexity and is required during the critical period for normal OD plasticity (Picard et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on cpg15.

claim: MHCI negatively regulates synapse development and deletion of MHCI or PirB enhances visual system plasticity in vivo.
source: Conversely, MHCI negatively regulates synapse development and deletion of MHCI or PirB, a MHCI receptor, enhances visual system plasticity in vivo (Cebrián et al., 2014; Shatz, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on MHCI and PirB.

claim: Spine formation and turnover is dramatically affected by MD in layer five cortical neurons.
source: Although the exact contribution of subtle changes in excitatory synapse density or morphology to visual circuit plasticity remains to be determined, Hofer et al., demonstrated that spine formation and turnover is dramatically affected by MD in layer five cortical neurons (Hofer et al., 2009), suggesting that an important functional correlation exists.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on spine dynamics during MD.

claim: Rem2 functions as a regulator of experience-dependent plasticity at the morphological, cellular and circuit levels.
source: Hence, our findings that Rem2 functions as a regulator of experience-dependent plasticity at the morphological, cellular and circuit levels provide an important step forward in connecting molecular regulators of neuronal morphology with broader circuit function.
evidence: Based on the collective findings regarding Rem2's role in spine morphology, intrinsic excitability, and OD plasticity.

claim: A primary function of Rem2 signaling is to stabilize the intrinsic excitability of cortical neurons in order to maintain proper levels of network activity.
source: In conclusion, our in vivo analysis of Rem2 in the visual system reveals that a primary function of Rem2 signaling is to stabilize the intrinsic excitability of cortical neurons in order to maintain proper levels of network activity.
evidence: Based on the collective findings regarding Rem2's role in regulating intrinsic excitability and spontaneous firing.

claim: Rem2 is expressed in other areas of the brain including the hippocampus, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens.
source: In addition to cortex, Rem2 is expressed in other areas of the brain including the hippocampus, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens (Ghiretti and Paradis, 2011; Liput et al., 2016), which are critical regions for learning, memory, and addiction.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work showing Rem2 expression patterns.

claim: Learning, memory, and addiction processes rely heavily on physiological and morphological plasticity at the level of individual neurons.
source: Interestingly, these processes rely heavily on physiological and morphological plasticity at the level of individual neurons (El-Gaby et al., 2015; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011; Martin et al., 2000; Yager et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on plasticity in learning, memory, and addiction.

claim: Rem2 likely acts in other brain regions and throughout the life of the animal, based on transcriptional profiling experiments performed in adult animals.
source: Therefore, it is likely that Rem2 acts in other brain regions and throughout the life of the animal, based on transcriptional profiling experiments performed in adult animals (Liput et al., 2016; Mardinly et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to transcriptional profiling studies showing Rem2 expression in adult animals.

claim: Rem2 functions at the nexus of a signaling network that senses and responds to changes in neuronal activity in order to preserve proper circuit function in the face of changing sensory experience.
source: Our data indicate that Rem2 functions at the nexus of a signaling network that senses and responds to changes in neuronal activity in order to preserve proper circuit function in the face of changing sensory experience.
evidence: Based on the collective findings regarding Rem2's activity-dependent expression and its role in regulating intrinsic excitability and circuit plasticity.

claim: Defining Rem2-dependent signaling mechanisms will elucidate the molecular mechanisms that instruct activity-dependent modifications of neural circuitry.
source: In the future, defining these Rem2-dependent signaling mechanisms will elucidate the molecular mechanisms that instruct activity-dependent modifications of neural circuitry.
evidence: Based on the importance of Rem2 in activity-dependent plasticity demonstrated in this study.
